compare_blocks.body:
Getting something done usually needs two kinds of work at once: pinning down the requirements so nothing is missed, and mapping the routes so nobody queues for nothing. (Fictional scene) Two jobs can be separated: one is verifying the known requirements — list, copies, stamps, deadlines, receipts; the other is finding out what else might exist — a second policy, outpatient benefits, accident benefits, an online channel, the review deadline. Who does which depends on who happens to hold the papers, who can get around this week, and who is willing to make the kind of call that involves a long wait.

Draw one line: whether it is covered, how much, and which proof is required are whatever the insurer's written reply and the policy say. Neither interprets the policy for the other, and neither concludes from hearsay. (Fictional scene) An aunt hears you are handling a claim, photographs a pile of receipts and says you know about this, do mine too. The same request, two legitimate responses. The other sets the scope first: I will list what you need to prepare, and ask me when you get stuck. The benefit is a clear boundary; the cost is being read as unhelpful.

An open-ended offer can leave more paperwork than the helper has time for. A narrower offer may sound abrupt unless the helper says what they can take on. Either person may choose either response, depending on their workload and relationship.

Agree on what help is wanted and who owns each step. In this example, the relative keeps responsibility for signing and submitting the claim.

The first misread is that ESTJ is more reliable and ENFP more quick-witted. Reliability is a delivery habit and quick-wittedness is another dimension; neither is the same thing as preference, and both can be trained.

The fourth takes E for sociable and good with people. E means attention and energy turn outward more often; either type may say little in a crowd, and either can organise a circle of people when needed.

compare_blocks.body:
Getting something done usually needs two kinds of work at once: pinning down the requirements so nothing is missed, and mapping the routes so nobody queues for nothing. These are not assigned by type but by who knows, who has time and who is willing; one person can do both. The two scenes below are fictional, used only to see how two points of attention meet.

### ENFP and ESTJ: claim documents — who checks the items, who maps the routes

(Fictional scene) Two jobs can be separated: one is verifying the known requirements — list, copies, stamps, deadlines, receipts; the other is finding out what else might exist — a second policy, outpatient benefits, accident benefits, an online channel, the review deadline. Who does which depends on who happens to hold the papers, who can get around this week, and who is willing to make the kind of call that involves a long wait.

Draw one line: whether it is covered, how much, and which proof is required are whatever the insurer's written reply and the policy say. Neither interprets the policy for the other, and neither concludes from hearsay. Replacing "this will definitely be covered" with "this condition is stated in clause whatever" makes the conversation more professional and saves a round of rework.

A check: photocopy the list twice — one copy to tick off progress, one to write after each item why it is required. The copy that stalls halfway usually marks where the two understandings diverge: one may know only that it must be submitted, the other why. The exercise checks whether understanding is aligned, not who resembles which type.

(Fictional scene) An aunt hears you are handling a claim, photographs a pile of receipts and says you know about this, do mine too. The same request, two legitimate responses. One agrees first: I will look at what the supplement notice is missing, you submit the documents, and I will walk you through the process. Agree on what help is wanted and who owns each step. In this example, the relative keeps responsibility for signing and submitting the claim.
